opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I finished my undergrad, I didn't have a clear picture at all. I was trained as a physicist, and I really loved physics, especially the way it tries to explain complicated phenomena with a few simple principles. But around that time deep learning was exploding, and I felt that something big was happening there, even if I couldn't say exactly what.

So my mindset was more like this: I didn't want to choose between physics and AI. I wanted to stand somewhere in the middle and see what each side could offer the other. One direction is "AI for physics": can we use neural networks to help scientists discover laws, find conserved quantities, or simplify models? The other direction, which I find even more interesting now, is "physics for AI": can we use the physicist's way of thinking to understand neural networks themselves? These are huge, messy systems with millions or billions of parameters, and that's very similar to what physicists face with many-body systems. We don't track every particle. We look for the right macroscopic variables, phase transitions, scaling laws, and so on.

At the time, though, it was mostly intuition and curiosity rather than a plan. I was lucky to end up in an environment where people were open to this kind of crossover work, so I could try lots of small projects and see what stuck. Looking back, the direction became clearer only after I'd done a few of them. But the core motivation was already there: I wanted AI to be something we can understand, not just something that works, and I felt physics gave me a good toolkit for that.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I finished my undergraduate degree in physics at Peking University, I honestly didn't see it as a choice between physics and AI. I saw them as two sides of the same question.

My training was in physics, and what I loved about physics was never really the specific systems. It was the way of thinking. Physicists look at something enormously complicated and ask: what are the few principles underneath that actually matter? Symmetry, conservation laws, scaling, phase transitions. These ideas let you compress a messy world into a handful of equations.

Around that time, deep learning was exploding, and what struck me was that neural networks felt exactly like the kind of system a physicist would want to study. Millions or billions of parameters, strange emergent behaviors, yet almost no theory explaining why they work. To me that looked like physics in the nineteenth century before thermodynamics, lots of engines running, nobody quite understanding the laws.

So I framed my direction as two arrows pointing in opposite directions. One arrow is AI for physics: can we use machine learning to discover conservation laws, symmetries, or governing equations from data, the way Kepler did by hand? The other arrow is physics for AI: can we borrow the physicist's toolkit to understand neural networks as physical objects, with their own phase transitions, their own scaling laws, their own notion of order and disorder?

I didn't want to pick one. I felt the most interesting things would happen exactly at the boundary, where methods from one side illuminate the other. That conviction is what led me to apply to MIT and work with Max Tegmark, because his group was one of the few places taking that boundary seriously rather than treating it as a side project. Looking back, I was lucky that the timing worked out, but at the time it mostly felt like following my own curiosity about why these systems behave the way they do.
